title: Design a Movie Ticket Booking System (OOD)
oneLiner: Shows, seat maps, holds that expire, and checkout, with one hard rule: a seat is never sold twice.
keyTakeaway: Seat status belongs to a seat in a particular show, not to the physical seat, and only one component may change it. Hold all requested seats or none in one critical section (a per-show lock in memory, a conditional UPDATE across servers), treat expired holds as free when checking, and authorise payment before confirming seats, capturing only after.
explanation:
Same format as the other OOD walk-throughs: write your answer for each stage first, then compare and tick what you covered. The parking lot walk-through explains what an OOD round grades.

What's specific to ticket booking. The class model itself is not hard (cinema, screen, seat, movie, show, booking), apart from one modelling decision interviewers watch for: availability is a property of a seat in one show, so it needs its own object (a ShowSeat). The real test is concurrency. Two people click the same seats at the same moment; a hold expires while someone is still typing their card number; a payment confirmation arrives late. The design has to keep "no seat sold twice" true in every one of those cases, and you have to show it in code.

Expect to discuss lock granularity (global, per show, per seat, and the deadlock risk of the last), pessimistic locking in memory versus optimistic conditional updates in a database, and why a distributed lock with a timeout shouldn't be the only guarantee. The model answer gives both an in-memory implementation and the SQL that keeps the same guarantee across many servers, behind one interface, and orders the payment steps so money and seats always agree.
